bridged_facts.statement: Self-supervised learning uses the data itself as supervision through pretext tasks such as reconstruction, rotation prediction, or jigsaw solving, in order to learn high-level semantic representations from large-scale unlabeled data; the modern instantiations of this idea fall into two families, contrastive learning and predictive learning.

Contrastive learning, named as one of the two modern self-supervised families, is introduced by first reinterpreting ordinary supervised classification as contrastive: a network splits into a classifier (the weights of the last fully-connected layer) and features (the representations produced just before that layer), so classification amounts to comparing features against per-class weight vectors.

Once the network is split into last-FC-layer classifier weights and the features before them, the comparison between features and class weights is exactly a contrastive objective: maximize similarities of positive pairs and minimize similarities of negative pairs.

Supervised classification realizes the maximize-positives / minimize-negatives objective using a predefined label vocabulary; when no such vocabulary exists, contrastive learning forms a vocabulary out of the data itself, letting each instance act as its own category.

MoCo instantiates the two-branch query/key contrastive pipeline with an asymmetric pair of encoders — the query encoder is updated by the loss gradient while the key encoder is a moving-average (momentum) copy — and this momentum update is one of two design choices for the key branch, the alternative being to share weights between both encoders.

Taking the weight-sharing option for the query/key branches yields the siamese variant of contrastive learning: both encoders share weights and both receive gradient updates, in contrast to the momentum moving-average key encoder.

Of the two modern self-supervised families, the predictive branch is illustrated first in NLP: masked language modeling as in BERT, where the model predicts the masked words (tokens) in the text so supervision comes from the text itself.

Masked image modeling in vision appears in two generations of backbone: the ConvNet-based context encoder that predicts masked patches by inpainting (CVPR 2016), and the Masked Autoencoder that predicts masked patches with Transformers (CVPR 2022).
The Transformer-based Masked Autoencoder operates not on raw pixels directly but on image patches treated as visual tokens, following the Vision Transformer formulation.

Given patches as visual tokens, MAE's pipeline randomly masks patches, encodes only the visible ones with a Transformer, expands the latents with learnable mask tokens so the decoder sees a full-length sequence, predicts the masked content, and computes an L2 loss in pixel space.

The claim that predicting a large portion of the input (rather than a small one) forces semantic features is backed up by the Input / MAE prediction / GT comparison, where a heavily masked image is reconstructed closely enough to match ground truth.

The heavy masking shown in the Input / MAE prediction / GT comparison is quantified as roughly 75% of an image being optimal, versus only about 15% of tokens in BERT-style language pretraining, because image information is far more redundant than linguistic information — so the masking ratio should be chosen per application.

Diffusion models generate images by gradually adding Gaussian noise and learning to reverse it, and this same denoising chain becomes text-conditioned generation when a caption (e.g. 'A golden lab puppy, tongue hanging out, and wearing a blue collar') is passed through a frozen text encoder to produce an embedding that guides the process, trained on caption-image pairs.
